“Now take the power that comes from above. A hailstone is a very small grain, yet when it falls on a man’s head, what pain it gives! Or again, take the drop that falls from the roof tile to the ground and bores a hole in the stone.

“You see, then, that the smallest things, falling from above onto the earth, have great power. So also the divine Spirit, coming from above, is powerful. Put your faith in this Spirit, then, and keep away from the other.”
orientation: The Shepherd gives Hermas the eleventh commandment and shows him a scene: believers on a bench and a false prophet on a chair. Hermas learns to test a prophet by the life he leads.

title: The two desires and the twelve commandments
english: The Shepherd said to me, “Take every evil desire away from yourself, and put on the desire that is good and honorable. For once you are clothed in this desire, you will hate evil desire, and you will bridle it just as you wish.

“Evil desire is wild and hard to tame. It is fearsome, and by its wildness it greatly consumes people. Above all, if a servant of God falls into it and has no understanding, it consumes him terribly. It consumes those who do not wear the garment of good desire but are entangled in this age. These it hands over to death.”

“Sir,” I said, “what are the works of evil desire that hand people over to death? Make them known to me, so that I may keep away from them.” “Listen,” he said, “to the works by which evil desire puts the servants of God to death.

“Foremost of all is the desire for another’s wife or husband, and for the extravagance of wealth, and for many vain delicacies and strong drink, and for many other foolish luxuries. For every luxury is foolish and empty for the servants of God.

“These desires, then, are evil, and they put the servants of God to death. For this evil desire is a daughter of the devil. So you must keep away from evil desires, so that by keeping away from them you may live to God.
“But all who are mastered by them and do not resist them will die utterly, for these desires are deadly.

“But you, put on the desire for righteousness. Arm yourself with the fear of the Lord, and resist them. For the fear of God dwells in good desire. If evil desire sees you armed with the fear of God and resisting it, it will flee far from you. It will not show itself to you again, because it fears your weapons.

“So when you have conquered evil desire and been crowned victor over it, come to the desire for righteousness. Hand over to her the victory you have won, and serve her just as she wishes. If you serve good desire and submit to her, you will be able to master evil desire and subdue it, just as you wish.”

“Sir,” I said, “I would like to know in what ways I must serve good desire.” “Listen,” he said. “Practice righteousness and virtue, truth and the fear of the Lord, faith and gentleness, and every good thing that is like these. If you practice these, you will be a servant well pleasing to God, and you will live to him. And everyone who serves good desire will live to God.”

So he finished the twelve commandments, and he said to me, “You have these commandments. Walk in them, and exhort those who hear, so that their repentance may be pure for the rest of the days of their life.

“Carry out with care this ministry that I am giving you, and you will accomplish much. For you will find favor with those who are going to repent, and they will heed your words. For I will be with you, and I will compel them to heed you.”

I said to him, “Sir, these commandments are great and good and glorious, and they can gladden the heart of anyone who is able to keep them. But I do not know whether these commandments can be kept by a human being, for they are very hard.”

He answered me, “If you make up your mind that they can be kept, you will keep them easily, and they will not be hard. But if the thought has already entered your heart that a human being cannot keep them, you will not keep them.

“But now I tell you: if you do not keep them, but neglect them, you will have no salvation, neither you nor your children nor your household. For you have already judged for yourself that these commandments cannot be kept by a human being.”
He said this to me in great wrath, so that I was thrown into confusion and was very much afraid of him. For his appearance was changed, so that no human being could have endured his wrath.

But when he saw me thoroughly shaken and confused, he began to speak to me more gently and more cheerfully. He said, “Foolish man, without understanding and double-minded! Do you not grasp the glory of God, how great and mighty and wonderful it is? For he created the world for the sake of man. He subjected all his creation to man, and gave him all authority to master everything under heaven.

“If, then,” he said, “man is lord of all God’s creatures and masters them all, can he not also master these commandments? The man who has the Lord in his heart can master all things, and every one of these commandments.
“But there are those who have the Lord on their lips, while their heart is hardened and they are far from the Lord. For them these commandments are hard, and rough to walk in.
“So you who are empty and light in the faith, put your Lord into your heart. Then you will know that nothing is easier than these commandments, nothing sweeter, and nothing gentler.
“Turn around, you who walk in the commandments of the devil, commandments that are harsh and bitter and wild and wanton. And do not fear the devil, for there is no power in him against you.
“For I will be with you, I, the angel of repentance, who have mastery over him. All the devil has is fear, and the fear of him has no strength. So do not fear him, and he will flee from you.”

I said to him, “Sir, hear a few words from me.” “Say what you wish,” he said. “Sir,” I said, “man is eager to keep the commandments of God. There is no one who does not ask the Lord to be made strong in his commandments and to submit to them. But the devil is hard, and he oppresses them.”

“He cannot oppress the servants of God who hope in God with their whole heart,” the Shepherd said. “The devil can wrestle against them, but he cannot wrestle them down. So if you resist him, he will be beaten, and he will flee from you in shame. But those who are half-empty,” he said, “fear the devil as though he had power.

“When a man has filled a great many jars with good wine, and a few among them are half-empty, he comes to the jars. He does not look at the full ones, for he knows that they are full. He looks at the half-empty ones, fearing that they have turned sour. For half-empty jars soon turn sour, and the flavor of the wine is lost.

“So too the devil comes to all the servants of God to test them. Those who are full in the faith resist him strongly, and he goes away from them, because he has no place where he can enter. So then he comes to the half-empty. There he has a place, and he enters them. He does in them whatever he wishes, and they become his slaves.
“But I, the angel of repentance, say to you: do not fear the devil. For I was sent,” he said, “to be with you who repent with your whole heart, and to make you strong in the faith.

“So believe God, you who have despaired of your life because of your sins, and who add to your sins and weigh down your life. Believe that if you turn to the Lord with your whole heart, and practice righteousness for the rest of the days of your life, and serve him rightly according to his will, he will heal your former sins. And you will have power to master the works of the devil. Do not fear the devil’s threat at all. It has no strength, like the sinews of a dead man.
“So listen to me. Fear the one who has all power, to save and to destroy. Keep these commandments, and you will live to God.”

I said to him, “Sir, now I have been made strong in all the ordinances of the Lord, because you are with me. I know that you will crush all the power of the devil, and that we will master him and prevail over all his works. And I hope, sir, that I am able to keep these commandments that you have given me, with the Lord making me strong.”
“You will keep them,” he said, “if your heart becomes pure toward the Lord. And all will keep them who cleanse their hearts from the vain desires of this age, and they will live to God.”
orientation: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance, gives Hermas the twelfth and last commandment: put away evil desire and put on good desire. He then closes the commandments and answers Hermas’s fear that they are too hard to keep.

title: Citizens of a far city must not invest in this foreign land
english: The Shepherd said to me, “You know that you, the servants of God, are living in a foreign land. For your own city is far from this city. If, then, you know your own city, the one where you are going to live, why do you prepare fields here, and costly furnishings, and buildings, and vain dwellings? Whoever prepares these things for this city cannot return to his own city.

“Foolish, double-minded, wretched man! Do you not grasp that all these things belong to another, and are under another’s authority? For the lord of this city will say, ‘I do not want you living in my city. Leave this city, for you do not live by my laws.’

“You have fields and dwellings and many other possessions. When he casts you out, what will you do with your field and your house and everything else that you have prepared for yourself? For the lord of this country justly says to you, ‘Either live by my laws, or leave my country.’

“What, then, are you going to do, you who have a law in your own city? For the sake of your fields and the rest of your possessions, will you deny your law altogether, and walk by the law of this city? Take care. It may prove unprofitable to deny your law. For if you wish to return to your own city, you will certainly not be received, because you denied the law of your city. You will be shut out of it.

“So take care. As one who lives in a foreign land, prepare nothing more for yourself than what is enough for your needs, and be ready. Then, when the master of this city wishes to cast you out for opposing his law, you can leave his city and go away to your own city. There you can live by your own law, rejoicing and free from insult.

“So take care, you who serve the Lord and have him in your heart. Do the works of God, remembering his commandments and the promises he made. Believe him, that he will keep his promises if his commandments are kept.

“So instead of fields, buy afflicted souls, each of you as he is able. Visit widows and orphans, and do not overlook them. Spend your wealth and all your furnishings, which you received from God, on fields and houses of this kind.

“For this is why the Master made you rich: so that you might carry out these ministries for him. It is far better to buy fields and possessions and houses of this kind, which you will find in your own city when you come home to it.
“This extravagance is good and sacred. It has no grief and no fear, but it has joy. So do not practice the extravagance of the nations, for it is unprofitable for you, the servants of God.

“Practice your own extravagance, in which you can rejoice. Do not counterfeit. Do not touch what belongs to another, and do not desire it, for it is evil to desire what belongs to others. Do your own work, and you will be saved.”
orientation: The commandments are finished, and the Shepherd now begins a series of parables. In this first one he tells the servants of God that they live in a foreign city and should not sink their wealth into it.

title: The parable of the elm and the vine
english: I was walking in the country, and I noticed an elm and a vine. I was considering them and their fruits when the Shepherd appeared to me. He said, “What are you turning over in your mind about the elm and the vine?” “Sir,” I said, “I am thinking how well they suit each other.”

“These two trees,” he said, “are set as a pattern for the servants of God.” “I would like to know,” I said, “the pattern of these trees you speak of.” “Do you see the elm and the vine?” he asked. “I see them, sir,” I said.

“This vine bears fruit,” he said, “but the elm is a tree without fruit. Yet unless this vine climbs up the elm, it lies cast on the ground and cannot bear much fruit. And the fruit it does bear is rotten, because it does not hang on the elm. So when the vine is cast upon the elm, it bears fruit both from itself and from the elm.

“So you see that the elm too gives much fruit, no less than the vine, and indeed even more.” “How does it give more, sir?” I asked. “Because,” he said, “when the vine hangs on the elm, it gives its fruit in plenty, and the fruit is good. But when it lies cast on the ground, it bears little, and that little is rotten. So this parable is set for the servants of God, for the poor man and the rich.”

“How so, sir?” I said. “Make it known to me.” “Listen,” he said. “The rich man has money, but in the things of the Lord he is poor, for his wealth distracts him. His intercession and his confession toward the Lord are very small. What he has is feeble and small, and has no other power.

“So when the rich man leans on the poor man and supplies him with what he needs, he believes that if he works for the poor man, he will be able to find his reward with God. For the poor man is rich in intercession and in confession, and his intercession has great power with God. So the rich man supplies the poor man with everything, without hesitation.

“And the poor man, supplied by the rich man, intercedes with God and gives him thanks for the one who gives to him. Then the rich man is still more zealous for the poor man, so that the poor man may be supplied without a break all his life. For he knows that the poor man’s intercession is acceptable and rich before the Lord.

“So both complete the work. The poor man works by his intercession, in which he is rich, and which he received from the Lord. He gives it back to the Lord who supplies him. And the rich man likewise, without hesitation, provides the poor man with the wealth that he received from the Lord. This is a great work, and acceptable with God. For the rich man has understood about his wealth, and has worked for the poor man out of the gifts of the Lord, and has carried out his ministry rightly.

“Now people suppose that the elm bears no fruit. They do not know, and they do not grasp, that when a drought comes, the elm holds water and feeds the vine. And the vine, having water without a break, gives double the fruit, both for itself and for the elm. So too the poor, by interceding with the Lord for the rich, make their wealth complete. And the rich in turn, by supplying the poor with what they need, make their prayers complete.
“So both become partners in the righteous work. Whoever does these things will not be forsaken by God, but will be written in the books of the living.
“Blessed are those who have possessions, and who understand that they are made rich by the Lord. For whoever understands this will also be able to carry out some good ministry.”
orientation: Farmers of the time trained their vines to climb elm trees. The Shepherd makes this a parable of how the rich and the poor help each other before God.

title: The winter of this age hides righteous and sinners alike
english: The Shepherd showed me many trees that had no leaves. They seemed to me to be dry, for they were all alike. He said to me, “Do you see these trees?” “I see them, sir,” I said. “They are all alike, and dry.” He answered me, “These trees that you see are the people who live in this age.”

“Then why, sir,” I asked, “do they seem dry, and all alike?” “Because,” he said, “in this age neither the righteous nor the sinners are plain to see. They are alike. For this age is winter for the righteous, and they are not plain to see, because they live among the sinners.

“In winter the trees have shed their leaves and are all alike, and it is not plain to see which are dry and which are living. In the same way, in this age neither the righteous nor the sinners are plain to see. All are alike.”
orientation: The Shepherd shows Hermas a stand of leafless trees. They picture how the righteous and the sinners cannot be told apart in this present age.

title: The fruit-bearing and the dry trees in the coming age
english: The Shepherd showed me many trees again, some budding and some dry. He said to me, “Do you see these trees?” “I see them, sir,” I said. “Some are budding, and some are dry.”

“These trees that are budding,” he said, “are the righteous, who are going to live in the age to come. For the age to come is summer for the righteous, but winter for sinners. So when the mercy of the Lord shines out, then those who serve God will be plainly seen, and all will be plainly seen.

“In summer the fruits of each tree are plainly seen, and it is known what kind they are. In the same way the fruits of the righteous will be plain to see, and all of them will be known to be flourishing in that age.

“But the nations and the sinners are the dry trees you saw. That is how they will be found in that age, dry and fruitless. They will be burned up like firewood, and they will be plain to see, because their conduct during their life was evil. The sinners will be burned because they sinned and did not repent. The nations will be burned because they did not know the one who created them.

“As for you, bear fruit, so that in that summer your fruit may be known. Keep away from many business affairs, and you will not sin in anything. For those who do much business also sin much. They are distracted by their business affairs, and they do not serve their Lord at all.

“How, then,” he said, “can such a man ask anything of the Lord and receive it, when he does not serve the Lord? Those who serve him will receive what they ask. But those who do not serve the Lord will receive nothing.
“But if a man works at one business only, he can serve the Lord as well. For his mind will not be corrupted and drawn away from the Lord. He will serve him with a pure mind.
“So if you do these things, you can bear fruit for the age to come. And whoever does these things will bear fruit.”
orientation: The Shepherd shows Hermas the trees again, some now budding and some dry. They picture the righteous and the sinners in the age to come.

title: The true fast and the parable of the vineyard
english: I was fasting, sitting on a certain mountain and giving thanks to the Lord for all that he had done for me, when I saw the Shepherd sitting beside me. He said, “Why have you come here so early in the morning?” “Because, sir,” I said, “I am keeping a station.”
“What is a station?” he asked. “I am fasting, sir,” I said. “And what is this fast that all of you are keeping?” he asked. “Sir,” I said, “I am fasting as I have been accustomed to do.”

“You do not know how to fast to the Lord,” he said. “This useless fast that you are keeping for him is no fast.” “Why do you say this, sir?” I asked. “I tell you,” he said, “this fast that all of you think you are keeping is not a fast. But I will teach you what a fast is that is acceptable to the Lord, and complete. Listen.
“God does not want a vain fast like this. For if you fast to God in this way, you will do nothing for righteousness. Fast to God, rather, in this way.

“Do nothing evil in your life, but serve the Lord with a pure heart. Keep his commandments and walk in his precepts, and let no evil desire arise in your heart. Believe God, that if you do these things, and fear him, and by self-control keep yourself from every evil deed, you will live to God. And if you do these things, you will keep a great fast, and one acceptable to God.
“Listen to the parable I am about to tell you. It has to do with fasting.

“A man had a field and many servants, and in one part of the field he planted a vineyard. He chose a certain servant who was faithful, well pleasing, and held in honor. He called him and said, ‘Take this vineyard that I have planted, and fence it with stakes until I come. Do nothing else to the vineyard. Keep this commandment of mine, and you will have your freedom from me.’ Then the servant’s master went away on his journey abroad.
“When he had gone, the servant took the vineyard and fenced it with stakes. And when he had finished fencing the vineyard, he saw that it was full of weeds.

“So he reasoned with himself. ‘I have carried out this commandment of my lord,’ he said. ‘Next I will dig this vineyard. It will be finer to look at once it is dug, and with no weeds it will give more fruit, because the weeds will not be choking it.’ He took it in hand and dug the vineyard, and pulled up all the weeds that were in it. And that vineyard became very fine to look at, and flourishing, with no weeds to choke it.

“After a time the master of the servant and of the field came, and he went into the vineyard. He saw the vineyard finely fenced, and dug as well, with all the weeds pulled up and the vines flourishing. And he was very glad at what the servant had done.

“So he called his beloved son, who was his heir, and his friends, who were his counselors. He told them all that he had commanded his servant, and all that he had found done. And they rejoiced with the servant at the testimony his master had given him.

“The master said to them, ‘I promised this servant his freedom if he kept the commandment I gave him. He has kept my commandment, and he has added a good work to the vineyard besides, and he has pleased me greatly. So in return for this work that he has done, I wish to make him joint heir with my son. For he thought of what was good, and he did not neglect it, but carried it out.’
“The master’s son agreed with him in this decision, that the servant should be joint heir with the son.

“A few days later the master gave a feast, and he sent the servant many dishes from the feast. The servant took the dishes that his master had sent him. He kept what was enough for himself, and shared out the rest among his fellow servants.
“His fellow servants were glad when they received the dishes. They began to pray for him, that he might find still greater favor with his master, because he had treated them in this way.

“His master heard all that had happened, and again he was very glad at what the servant had done. The master called his friends and his son together once more, and told them what the servant had done with the dishes he had received. And they agreed all the more that the servant should be made joint heir with his son.”
I said, “Sir, I do not understand these parables, and I cannot grasp them unless you explain them to me.”

“I will explain everything to you,” he said, “and all that I speak of with you. I will show you his commandments. And if you do any good thing beyond what God has commanded, you will win greater glory for yourself, and you will be more glorious before God than you were going to be. So if you keep the commandments of God and add these services as well, you will rejoice, if you keep them according to my commandment.”

I said to him, “Sir, whatever you command me, I will keep it, for I know that you are with me.” “I will be with you,” he said, “because you are so eager to do good. And I will be with all who have this same eagerness.
“This fast is very good,” he said, “when the commandments of the Lord are kept. So this is how you shall keep the fast that you are about to keep.
“First of all, guard yourself against every evil word and every evil desire, and cleanse your heart of all the vanities of this age. If you keep these things, this fast of yours will be perfect.

“And this is what you shall do. When you have done all that is written here, on the day that you fast, taste nothing but bread and water. Reckon up what you would have spent on the food you were going to eat that day, and give it to a widow, or an orphan, or someone in need. In this way you will be humble in mind, so that through your humility the one who receives may fill his soul, and pray to the Lord for you.

“So if you carry out the fast in this way, as I have commanded you, your sacrifice will be acceptable to God, and this fast will be written down. And the service done in this way is good and cheerful, and well pleasing to the Lord.

“You shall keep these things in this way, you with your children and your whole household. If you keep them, you will be blessed. And all who hear them and keep them will be blessed, and whatever they ask of the Lord, they will receive.”

I begged him earnestly to make clear to me the parable of the field and the master, the vineyard and the servant who fenced it, the stakes, the weeds pulled up out of the vineyard, the son, and the friends who were his counselors. For I understood that all these things were a parable.

He answered me, “You are very presumptuous with your questions. You ought not to ask anything at all. For if a thing needs to be made clear to you, it will be made clear.” I said to him, “Sir, whatever you show me and do not make clear, I will have seen in vain, without grasping what it is. In the same way, if you tell me parables and do not explain them to me, I will have heard something from you in vain.”

He answered me again, “Whoever is a servant of God and has his Lord in his heart asks him for understanding, and receives it. He explains every parable, and the words of the Lord that are spoken in parables become known to him. But those who are feeble and idle in making petition hesitate to ask the Lord.

“Yet the Lord is full of compassion, and he gives without ceasing to all who ask him. But you have been made strong by the holy angel. You have received from him such a gift of petition, and you are not idle. Why, then, do you not ask the Lord for understanding, and receive it from him?”

I said to him, “Sir, since I have you with me, it is you I must ask, and you I must question. For you show me everything, and you speak with me. If I were seeing or hearing these things without you, I would ask the Lord that they be made clear to me.”

“I told you just now,” he said, “that you are crafty and presumptuous, asking for the explanations of the parables. But since you are so persistent, I will explain to you the parable of the field, and all the rest that goes with it, so that you may make these things known to everyone. Listen now,” he said, “and understand them.

“The field is this world. The lord of the field is the one who created all things, and completed them, and gave them strength. The servant is the Son of God. The vines are this people, whom he himself planted.

“The stakes are the holy angels of the Lord, who hold his people together. The weeds pulled up out of the vineyard are the lawless deeds of the servants of God. The dishes that he sent him from the feast are the commandments that he gave to his people through his Son. The friends and counselors are the holy angels who were created first. And the master’s journey abroad is the time that remains until his coming.”

I said to him, “Sir, all this is great and wonderful, and all of it is glorious. Could I, then, have grasped these things? No other human being can grasp them either, even one with great understanding. One thing more, sir,” I said. “Make clear to me what I am about to ask you.”
“Speak,” he said, “if there is something you wish.” “Sir,” I said, “why is the Son of God set in the parable in the guise of a servant?”
“Listen,” he said. “The Son of God is not set in the guise of a servant. He is set in great authority and lordship.” “How so, sir?” I said. “I do not grasp it.”

“Because God planted the vineyard,” he said. “That is, he created the people, and handed them over to his Son. And the Son appointed the angels over them, to keep watch over them. And he himself cleansed their sins, laboring much and bearing many toils. For no vineyard can be dug without toil or hardship.
“So when he himself had cleansed the sins of the people, he showed them the paths of life, and gave them the law that he received from his Father.
“But listen to why the Lord took his Son and the glorious angels as counselors about the servant’s inheritance.

“God made the Holy Spirit, who existed before and who created the whole creation, to dwell in flesh that he chose. So this flesh, in which the Holy Spirit dwelt, served the Spirit well. It walked in reverence and purity, and did not defile the Spirit in any way.

“So this flesh lived well and purely. It labored with the Spirit and worked with him in everything, and it conducted itself with strength and courage. Therefore God chose it as a partner with the Holy Spirit. For the way this flesh walked was pleasing, because it was not defiled on earth while it had the Holy Spirit.

“So he took the Son and the glorious angels as counselors, so that this flesh too, which had served the Spirit blamelessly, might have some place to dwell, and might not seem to have lost the reward of its service. For all flesh in which the Holy Spirit has dwelt will receive a reward, if it is found undefiled and spotless.
“Now you have the explanation of this parable as well.”

“Sir,” I said, “I was glad to hear this explanation.” “Now listen,” he said. “Keep this flesh of yours pure and undefiled, so that the Spirit that dwells in it may bear witness to it, and your flesh may be justified.

“Take care that it never enters your heart that this flesh of yours is perishable, and that you never misuse it in some defilement. If you defile your flesh, you will defile the Holy Spirit as well. And if you defile the flesh, you will not live.”

“But sir,” I said, “if there was some ignorance in the past, before these words were heard, how is the man to be saved who has defiled his flesh?” “For former deeds of ignorance,” he said, “God alone can give healing, for all authority is his, provided that from now on you defile neither your flesh nor the Spirit. For the two belong together, and neither can be defiled without the other. So keep both pure, and you will live to God.”
orientation: Hermas is keeping a “station,” an early Christian word for a day set aside for fasting. The Shepherd teaches him what kind of fast God accepts, tells a parable about a master, his servant and a vineyard, and then explains it.

title: The two shepherds: luxury and punishment
english: I was sitting in my house, glorifying the Lord for all I had seen, and pondering the commandments: how good they are, and powerful, and joyful, and glorious, and able to save a person’s soul. I said to myself, “I will be blessed if I walk in these commandments, and whoever walks in them will be blessed.”

While I was saying this to myself, I suddenly saw the Shepherd sitting beside me, and he said, “Why are you double-minded about the commandments I gave you? They are good. Do not be double-minded at all, but put on the faith of the Lord, and you will walk in them. For I will give you strength in them.
“These commandments benefit those who are going to repent. For if they do not walk in them, their repentance is in vain.

“So you who are repenting, throw off the evils of this age that wear you down. When you have put on every virtue of righteousness, you will be able to keep these commandments and to add no more to your sins. Walk, then, in these commandments of mine, and you will live to God. All these things I have spoken to you.”

When he had finished speaking with me, he said, “Let us go into the country, and I will show you the shepherds of the sheep.” “Let us go, sir,” I said. We came to a plain, and he showed me a young shepherd dressed in a suit of saffron-colored clothes.

He was pasturing a great many sheep, and these sheep seemed to be living in luxury and indulging themselves to the full. They were cheerful, skipping here and there. The shepherd himself was very cheerful over his flock. His whole appearance was very cheerful, and he ran about among the sheep.

The Shepherd said to me, “Do you see this shepherd?” “I see him, sir,” I said. “This,” he said, “is the angel of luxury and deceit. He wears down the souls of the servants of God and turns them away from the truth. He deceives them with evil desires, and in those desires they are destroyed.
“For they forget the commandments of the living God and walk in deceits and empty luxuries. And they are destroyed by this angel, some to death and some to corruption.”

I said to him, “Sir, I do not know what ‘to death’ means, or what ‘to corruption’ means.” “Listen,” he said. “The sheep you saw cheerful and skipping are those who have been torn away from God completely and have handed themselves over to the desires of this age. For these there is no repentance that leads to life, because they have added to their sins and have blasphemed against the name of God. To such people, then, death belongs.

“But the sheep you saw that were not skipping, but feeding in one place, are those who have handed themselves over to luxuries and deceits, yet have spoken no blasphemy against the Lord. These, then, have been corrupted from the truth. For these there is hope of repentance, and by it they can live. Corruption, then, has hope of some renewal, but death has eternal destruction.”

Again I went on a little way, and he showed me a large shepherd who looked almost wild. He was wrapped in a white goatskin. He had a bag on his shoulders, and a very hard staff with knots in it, and a great whip. His look was so bitter that I was afraid of him. Such was the look he had.

This shepherd was taking from the young shepherd the sheep that were indulging themselves and living in luxury, but not skipping. He threw them into a place that was steep and full of thorns and thistles, so that the sheep could not get free of the thorns and thistles, but were tangled in them.

So these sheep, tangled as they were, fed among the thorns and thistles, and they were in great misery, for he was beating them. He drove them about, here and there, and gave them no rest, and those sheep had no ease at all.
When I saw them whipped like this and in such misery, I grieved for them, because they were so tormented and had no relief at all.

I said to the Shepherd who was speaking with me, “Sir, who is this shepherd, so pitiless and bitter, who has no compassion at all for these sheep?” “This,” he said, “is the angel of punishment. He is one of the righteous angels, but he is set over punishment.
“So he takes those who wander away from God and have walked in the desires and deceits of this age, and he punishes them as they deserve, with terrible and varied punishments.”

“Sir,” I said, “I would like to know what these varied punishments are.” “Listen,” he said, “to the varied torments and punishments. The torments belong to this life. Some are punished with losses, some with want, some with varied illnesses, and some with unrest of every kind. Others are insulted by unworthy people and suffer in many other ways.

“For many are restless in their plans. They set their hand to many things, and nothing at all goes forward for them. They say that they do not prosper in what they do, and it does not enter their heart that they have done evil deeds. Instead they blame the Lord.

“So when they have been afflicted with every tribulation, then they are handed over to me for good discipline. They are made strong in the faith of the Lord, and for the rest of the days of their life they serve the Lord with a pure heart.

“And if they repent, then the evil deeds they did enter their heart, and then they glorify God. They say that he is a righteous judge, and that each of them suffered justly, according to his deeds. From then on they serve the Lord with a pure heart, and they prosper in all they do, receiving from the Lord everything they ask. And then they glorify the Lord because they were handed over to me, and they no longer suffer any evil.”

I said to him, “Sir, explain this also to me.” “What are you asking?” he said. “Sir,” I said, “are those who live in luxury and are deceived tormented for the same length of time that they live in luxury and are deceived?” He said to me, “They are tormented for the same length of time.”
“Sir,” I said, “they are tormented very little. Those who live in such luxury and forget God ought to be tormented seven times over.”

He said to me, “You are foolish, and you do not understand the power of torment.” “If I understood it, sir,” I said, “I would not be asking you to explain it to me.” “Listen,” he said, “to the power of both.

“The time of luxury and deceit is one hour, but an hour of torment has the power of thirty days. So if someone lives in luxury and is deceived for one day, and is tormented for one day, the day of torment has the force of a whole year. For as many days as someone lives in luxury, then, for so many years he is tormented. So you see,” he said, “that the time of luxury and deceit is very short, but the time of punishment and torment is long.”
“Sir,” I said, “I still do not understand at all about the time of deceit and luxury and torment. Explain it to me more clearly.”

He answered me, “Your foolishness stays with you, and you are not willing to cleanse your heart and serve God. Take care,” he said, “that the time is not fulfilled and you are found foolish. Listen, then, as you wish, so that you may understand these things.

“The one who lives in luxury and is deceived for a single day, and does what he wants, has put on great foolishness and does not understand what he is doing. By the next day he forgets what he did the day before, for luxury and deceit have no memories, because of the foolishness he has put on. But when punishment and torment cling to a person for a single day, he is punished and tormented for as long as a year, for punishment and torment have long memories.

“So when he has been tormented and punished for the whole year, he then remembers the luxury and deceit, and he knows that because of them he is suffering these evils. Every person, then, who lives in luxury and is deceived is tormented in this way, because, though they have life, they have handed themselves over to death.”

“Sir,” I said, “what kinds of luxury are harmful?” “Every act a person does with pleasure,” he said, “is luxury to him. Even the angry man lives in luxury when he satisfies his own passion. The adulterer, the drunkard, the slanderer, the liar, the greedy man, the cheat, and whoever does things like these, each satisfies his own sickness. So he lives in luxury in what he does.
“All these luxuries are harmful to the servants of God. It is because of these deceits, then, that those who are punished and tormented suffer.

“But there are also luxuries that save people. For many who do good live in luxury, carried along by their own pleasure. This luxury, then, benefits the servants of God and brings life to such a person. But the harmful luxuries I named before bring them torments and punishments. And if they persist and do not repent, they bring death on themselves.”
orientation: Hermas is at home thinking over the commandments when the Shepherd appears and takes him out to a plain. There the Shepherd shows him two other shepherds: a cheerful young one, who is the angel of luxury and deceit, and a fierce one, who is the angel of punishment.

title: The head of the house must be afflicted so the household may repent
english: A few days later I saw the Shepherd in the same plain where I had seen the shepherds, and he said to me, “What are you seeking?”
“Sir,” I said, “I am here so that you may order the punishing shepherd to leave my house, for he afflicts me greatly.”
“You must be afflicted,” he said. “For this is what the glorious angel has commanded concerning you. He wants you to be tested.”
“But what have I done, sir,” I said, “that is so evil that I should be handed over to this angel?”

“Listen,” he said. “Your sins are many, but not so many that you should be handed over to this angel. But your household has committed great acts of lawlessness and sin, and the glorious angel was bitterly provoked by what they did. That is why he ordered you to be afflicted for a time, so that they too may repent and cleanse themselves of every desire of this age. So when they repent and are cleansed, then the angel of punishment will depart from you.”
I said to him, “Sir, if they have done such things that the glorious angel is bitterly provoked, what have I done?”

“There is no other way for them to be afflicted,” he said, “unless you, the head of the house, are afflicted. For when you are afflicted, they too are bound to be afflicted. But while you are at ease, they can have no tribulation.”
“But look, sir,” I said, “they have repented with their whole heart.”

“I know it too,” he said. “They have repented with their whole heart. But do you think that the sins of those who repent are forgiven at once? Not at all. The one who repents must torment his own soul. He must be deeply humble in all he does, and be afflicted with tribulations of every kind. And if he bears the tribulations that come upon him, the one who created all things and gave them strength will surely be moved with compassion and will give him some healing.

“And he will surely do this, if he sees that the heart of the one who repents is pure of every evil thing. But it is to your benefit, and your household’s, to be afflicted now. Why should I say more to you? You must be afflicted, as that angel of the Lord commanded, the one who handed you over to me. And give thanks to the Lord for this: he counted you worthy to be shown the tribulation beforehand, so that, knowing of it in advance, you may bear it with strength.”
I said to him, “Sir, be with me, and I will be able to bear every tribulation.”

“I will be with you,” he said. “I will also ask the punishing angel to afflict you more lightly. Still, you will be afflicted for a little while, and then you will be restored to your house. Only continue to be humble and to minister to the Lord with a wholly pure heart, you and your children and your household. Walk in my commandments, which I am giving you, and your repentance can be strong and pure.
“And if you keep these commandments together with your household, every tribulation will depart from you. Yes,” he said, “and tribulation will depart from all who walk in these commandments of mine.”
orientation: A few days later Hermas meets the Shepherd in the same plain and asks him to send away the angel of punishment, who is now in his own house. The Shepherd explains why Hermas must suffer for a time.

title: The great willow and the rods
english: The Shepherd showed me a great willow that sheltered plains and mountains, and all who are called by the name of the Lord had come under the shelter of the willow.

Beside the willow stood an angel of the Lord, glorious and very tall, holding a great sickle. He was cutting branches from the willow and giving them to the people sheltered by the willow. He gave them little rods, about a cubit long.
When all had received their little rods, the angel laid down the sickle, and the tree was whole, just as I had seen it before.

I marveled and said to myself, “How can the tree be whole when so many branches have been cut off?” The Shepherd said to me, “Do not marvel that this tree has stayed whole after so many branches were cut off. But when you have seen everything,” he said, “it will be made clear to you what this is.”

The angel who had given the rods to the people asked for them back. They were called to him in the same order in which they had received them, and each one of them gave back the rods. The angel of the Lord took the rods and examined them.
From some he received rods that were dry and eaten, as if by moths. The angel ordered those who had handed in such rods to stand apart.
Others handed in rods that were dry but not eaten by moths, and he ordered these also to stand apart.
Others handed in rods that were half dry, and these stood apart.
Others handed in their rods half dry and with cracks in them, and these stood apart.
Others handed in their rods green and with cracks in them, and these stood apart.
Others handed in rods of which one half was dry and the other half green, and these stood apart.
Others brought their rods with two thirds of the rod green and one third dry, and these stood apart.
Others handed in rods two thirds dry and one third green, and these stood apart.
Others handed in their rods almost wholly green. Only the smallest part of their rods was dry, the very tip, but the rods had cracks in them. These too stood apart.
The rods of others had only the smallest part green, and the rest was dry, and these stood apart.

Others came bringing their rods green, just as they had received them from the angel. The greater part of the crowd handed in rods like these. The angel rejoiced greatly over them, and these stood apart.
Others handed in their rods green and with shoots on them, and these stood apart. Over these too the angel rejoiced greatly.

Others handed in their rods green and with shoots, and their shoots bore something like fruit. The people whose rods were found like this were very cheerful. The angel exulted over them, and the Shepherd was very cheerful over them.

Then the angel of the Lord ordered crowns to be brought. Crowns were brought, made, it seemed, of palm. He crowned the men who had handed in the rods with shoots and some fruit, and he sent them off into the tower.
He also sent the others into the tower, those who had handed in their rods green and with shoots, but with no fruit on the shoots. To them he gave seals.
All who went into the tower had the same clothing, white as snow.
Those who had handed in their rods green, just as they had received them, he also sent off, and he gave them clothing and seals.

When the angel had finished all this, he said to the Shepherd, “I am going away. You are to send these within the walls, each to dwell where he is worthy to dwell. But examine their rods carefully, and then send them off. Examine them carefully. See that no one slips past you,” he said. “But if anyone does slip past you, I will test them at the altar.” Having said this to the Shepherd, he went away.
After the angel had gone, the Shepherd said to me, “Let us take the rods from all of them and plant them, to see whether any of them can live.” I said to him, “Sir, how can these dry things live?”

He answered me, “This tree is a willow, and its kind loves life. So if the rods are planted and get a little moisture, many of them will live. After that, let us try pouring water on them as well. If any of them is able to live, I will rejoice with them. But if one does not live, I at least will not be found careless.”

The Shepherd told me to call them, each in the order in which he had stood. They came group by group and handed their rods to the Shepherd. The Shepherd took the rods and planted them, group by group. After planting them, he poured so much water over them that the rods could not be seen for the water.

When he had watered the rods, he said to me, “Let us go. In a few days let us come back and look at all the rods. For the one who created this tree wants all who have received branches from this tree to live. And I too hope that these little rods, now that they have taken in moisture and been watered, will live, the greater part of them.”

I said to him, “Sir, tell me what this tree is. I am puzzled about it, because so many branches have been cut off and yet the tree is whole, and nothing appears to have been cut from it. That is what puzzles me.”

“Listen,” he said. “This great tree that shelters plains and mountains and all the earth is the law of God, which was given to the whole world. And this law is the Son of God, proclaimed to the ends of the earth. The peoples under its shelter are those who heard the proclamation and believed in him.

“The great and glorious angel is Michael, who has authority over this people and governs them. For he is the one who gives them the law, into the hearts of those who believe. So he inspects those to whom he gave it, to see whether they have kept it.

“You see the rods of each one, for the rods are the law. You see, then, that many rods have been made useless, and you will come to know all those who did not keep the law. And you will see the dwelling of each one.”

I said to him, “Sir, why did he send some off into the tower and leave others to you?” “All who broke the law that they received from him,” he said, “he left under my authority, for repentance. But all who have already satisfied the law and kept it, he keeps under his own authority.”

“Then who, sir,” I said, “are those who were crowned and are going into the tower?” “All who wrestled with the devil and overcame him,” he said, “are the ones who were crowned. These are the ones who suffered for the law.
“The others, who also handed in their rods green and with shoots, but without fruit, are those who were afflicted for the law but did not suffer, and did not deny their law.

“Those who handed in their rods green, just as they received them, are reverent and righteous. They have walked with a very pure heart and have kept the commandments of the Lord. The rest you will learn when I examine these rods that have been planted and watered.”

A few days later we came to the place. The Shepherd sat down in the angel’s place, and I stood beside him. He said to me, “Tie a towel around your waist and serve me.” So I tied on a clean towel made of sackcloth.

When he saw that I had the towel on and was ready to serve him, he said, “Call the men whose rods have been planted, group by group, in the order in which each handed in his rods.” I went out to the plain and called them all, and they all stood there, group by group.
The Shepherd said to them, “Let each one pull up his own rods and bring them to me.”
The first to hand theirs in were those whose rods had been dry and eaten. As their rods were found dry and eaten, he ordered them to stand apart.

Then those whose rods had been dry but not eaten handed theirs in. Some of them handed in their rods green, and some handed them in dry and eaten, as if by moths. Those who handed in green rods he ordered to stand apart. Those who handed in rods dry and eaten he ordered to stand with the first group.

Then those whose rods had been half dry and cracked handed theirs in. Many of them handed in rods that were green and had no cracks. Some handed in rods green and with shoots, and with fruit on the shoots, such as those had who went crowned into the tower. But some handed in rods dry and eaten, some dry but not eaten, and some just as they had been, half dry and cracked. He ordered each one of them to stand apart, some with their own groups and some by themselves.

Then those whose rods had been green but cracked handed theirs in. All of these handed in green rods, and they stood in their own group. The Shepherd rejoiced over them, because they had all been changed and had put away their cracks.

Those whose rods had been half green and half dry also handed theirs in. The rods of some were found wholly green, of some half dry, of some dry and eaten, and of some green and with shoots. All these were sent off, each to his own group.

Then those whose rods had been two thirds green and one third dry handed theirs in. Many of them handed in green rods, many handed in half-dry rods, and others rods that were dry and eaten. All these stood in their own group.

Then those whose rods had been two thirds dry and one third green handed theirs in. Many of them handed in half-dry rods, some handed in rods dry and eaten, others rods half dry and cracked, and a few handed in green rods. All these stood in their own group.

Those whose rods had been green, with only the smallest part dry, and cracked, also handed theirs in. Some of these handed in green rods, and some green rods with shoots. These too went off to their group.

Then those whose rods had had only the smallest part green, and the rest dry, handed theirs in. Most of their rods were found green and with shoots, and with fruit on the shoots, and the others wholly green. Over these rods the Shepherd rejoiced very greatly, because they were found like this. And these went off, each to his own group.

When the Shepherd had examined everyone’s rods, he said to me, “I told you that this tree loves life. Do you see,” he said, “how many have repented and been saved?” “I see, sir,” I said. “It is so that you may see the abounding compassion of the Lord,” he said, “how great and glorious it is. And he has given the Spirit to those who were worthy of repentance.”

“Why then, sir,” I said, “did they not all repent?” “He gave repentance,” he said, “to those whose heart he saw was going to become pure, and who were going to serve him with their whole heart. But to those in whom he saw guile and wickedness, who were going to repent in hypocrisy, he gave no repentance, so that they might not profane his name again.”

I said to him, “Sir, now explain to me about those who handed in the rods, what kind of person each of them is, and where they dwell. Then those who believed and received the seal, but have broken it and not kept it whole, may hear this, recognize their own deeds, and repent. They may receive a seal from you and glorify the Lord, because he had compassion on them and sent you to renew their spirits.”

“Listen,” he said. “Those whose rods were found dry and eaten by moths are the apostates and betrayers of the church. In their sins they blasphemed the Lord, and more than that, they were ashamed of the name of the Lord that was called upon them. These, then, have perished completely to God. And you see that not one of them repented, though they heard the words you spoke to them, the words I commanded you. From such people life has departed.

“Those who handed in rods that were dry but not rotten are close to them. For they were hypocrites, who brought in strange teachings and turned the servants of God aside, especially those who had sinned. They would not let them repent, but persuaded them with their foolish teachings. These, then, have hope of repenting.

“And you see that many of them have indeed repented since I told them my commandments, and they will yet repent. But all who will not repent have lost their life. Those of them who did repent became good, and their dwelling was within the first walls, and some even went up into the tower. So you see,” he said, “that repentance from sins has life in it, but not to repent has death.
“Hear also about those who handed in rods half dry and with cracks in them. Those whose rods were half dry are the double-minded, for they are neither alive nor dead.

“Those whose rods were half dry and had cracks in them are both double-minded and slanderers. They are never at peace among themselves, but always in dissension. Yet for these too,” he said, “repentance is at hand. You see that some of them have repented, and still there is hope of repentance in them.

“All of them who have repented,” he said, “will have their dwelling in the tower. Those of them who have repented more slowly will dwell within the walls. But those who do not repent, and persist in their deeds, will surely die.

“Those who handed in their rods green but with cracks in them were always faithful and good, yet they had a certain rivalry among themselves over first place and over some kind of honor. But all these are fools, to have rivalry among themselves over first place.

“Yet these too, because they were good, cleansed themselves and repented quickly when they heard my commandments. So their dwelling was in the tower. But if any of them returns to dissension, he will be thrown out of the tower and will lose his life.

“Life belongs to all who keep the commandments of the Lord. And in the commandments there is nothing about first place or any kind of honor, but about patience and a man’s humility. In such people, then, is the life of the Lord, but in those who stir up dissension and break the law there is death.
“Those who handed in their rods half green and half dry are those who are tangled up in their business affairs and do not hold fast to the saints. That is why half of them is alive and half is dead.

“Many of them, then, repented when they heard my commandments. All who repented have their dwelling in the tower. But some of them fell away completely. These have no repentance, for because of their business affairs they blasphemed the Lord and denied him. So they lost their life through the wickedness they did.

“But many of them were double-minded. For these there is still repentance, if they repent quickly, and their dwelling will be in the tower. If they repent more slowly, they will dwell within the walls. But if they do not repent, they too have lost their life.
“Those who handed in rods two thirds green and one third dry are those who have denied, with denials of many kinds.

“Many of them, then, repented and went away to dwell in the tower. But many fell away from God completely, and these have lost their life completely. Some of them were double-minded and fell into dissension. For these, then, there is repentance, if they repent quickly and do not persist in their pleasures. But if they persist in their deeds, they too are working death for themselves.

“Those who handed in rods two thirds dry and one third green are those who had become faithful, but then grew rich and came to be honored among the nations. They put on great pride and became haughty. They left the truth and did not hold fast to the righteous, but lived together with the nations, and this path became sweeter to them. Yet they did not fall away from God. They stayed in the faith, though they did not do the works of the faith.
“Many of them, then, repented, and their dwelling was in the tower.
“But others lived altogether with the nations and were corrupted by the empty glories of the nations. They fell away from God and did the deeds of the nations. These were counted with the nations.

“Others of them were double-minded, having no hope of being saved because of the deeds they had done. And others were double-minded and made divisions among themselves. For these who were double-minded because of their deeds there is still repentance. But their repentance must be swift, so that their dwelling may be in the tower. As for those who do not repent but persist in their pleasures, death is near.

“Those who handed in their rods green, but with the very tips dry and cracked, were always good and faithful and honored before God. But they sinned a very little, through small desires and through holding small things against one another. When they heard my words, the greater part of them repented quickly, and their dwelling was in the tower.

“But some of them were double-minded, and some, being double-minded, caused greater dissension. In these, then, there is hope of repentance, because they were always good, and hardly any of them will die.

“Those who handed in their rods dry, with only the smallest part green, are those who believed, and no more, but did the works of lawlessness. Yet they never fell away from God. They bore the name gladly, and gladly welcomed the servants of God into their houses. So when they heard of this repentance, they repented without hesitation, and they are practicing every virtue and righteousness.
“Some of them are also afraid, knowing the deeds they have done. The dwelling of all these, then, will be in the tower.”

When he had finished explaining all the rods, he said to me, “Go and tell everyone to repent and live to God. For the Lord had compassion and sent me to give repentance to all, though some are not worthy because of their deeds. But the Lord is patient, and he wants those who were called through his Son to be saved.”
I said to him, “Sir, I hope that all who hear these things will repent. For I am persuaded that each one, when he recognizes his own deeds and fears God, will repent.”

He answered me, “All who repent with their whole heart, and cleanse themselves of the wicked deeds I have named, and add nothing more to their sins, will receive from the Lord healing for their former sins. That is, if they are not double-minded about these commandments. And they will live to God. But all who add to their sins,” he said, “and walk in the desires of this age, will condemn themselves to death.
“But as for you, walk in my commandments, and you will live to God. And all who walk in them and do what is right will live to God.”
When he had shown me all these things and told me all of them, he said to me, “The rest I will show you in a few days.”
orientation: The Shepherd shows Hermas a great willow, from which an angel cuts a rod for each person and later asks for it back; the state of each rod shows the state of the one who held it. The rods are examined twice: when they are first handed back, and again after the Shepherd has planted and watered them.

title: The Shepherd shows Hermas the twelve mountains and the tower's foundation stones
english: After I had written down the commandments and parables of the Shepherd, the angel of repentance, he came to me. “I want to show you,” he said, “all that the Holy Spirit showed you, the Spirit that spoke with you in the form of the Church. For that Spirit is the Son of God.

“You were too weak in the flesh, and so it was not made clear to you through an angel. But when you were given power through the Spirit and grew strong in your strength, so that you could see even an angel, then the building of the tower was revealed to you through the Church. You saw everything well and reverently, as shown by a virgin. Now you see it shown by an angel, though through the same Spirit.

“But you must learn everything more exactly from me. This is why the glorious angel gave me to dwell in your house: so that you might see everything with strength, and not be afraid of anything as you were before.”

And he led me away to Arcadia, to a rounded mountain. He sat me down on the top of the mountain and showed me a great plain. Around the plain were twelve mountains, and each mountain was different in appearance.
The first was black as soot. The second was bare, with no plants on it. The third was full of thorns and thistles.
The fourth had plants that were half dry. The tops of the plants were green, but the parts near the roots were dry. And some of the plants dried up whenever the sun scorched them.

The fifth mountain had green plants, and it was rough. The sixth mountain was full of cracks all over, some small and some large. There were plants in the cracks, but the plants were not very flourishing. They looked more as if they had withered.

The seventh mountain had cheerful plants, and the whole mountain was thriving. Every kind of cattle and bird fed on that mountain, and the more the cattle and the birds fed, the more and more the plants of that mountain flourished. The eighth mountain was full of springs, and every kind of the Lord’s creatures drank from the springs of that mountain.

The ninth mountain had no water at all and was desolate throughout. On it were wild beasts and deadly reptiles that destroy people. The tenth mountain had very great trees and was all in shade, and under the shelter of the trees sheep lay resting and chewing the cud.

The eleventh mountain was very thick with trees, and those trees were laden with fruit. They were adorned with fruit of one kind and another, so that anyone who saw them would long to eat of their fruit. The twelfth mountain was all white, and its look was cheerful. The mountain in itself was most beautiful.
In the middle of the plain he showed me a great white rock that had risen up out of the plain. The rock was higher than the mountains, and square, so that it could hold the whole world.
That rock was old, and a gate had been cut out of it. But the carving of the gate seemed to me to be recent. The gate shone so much brighter than the sun that I marveled at the radiance of the gate.

Around the gate stood twelve virgins. The four who stood at the corners seemed to me the more glorious, but the others were glorious too. They stood at the four sides of the gate, and between them stood the others, two by two.
They wore linen tunics and were beautifully girded, with their right shoulders bare, as if they were about to carry some load. That is how ready they were, for they were very cheerful and eager.

When I had seen these things, I marveled within myself, because I was seeing great and glorious things. And then I was perplexed about the virgins. Delicate as they were, they stood bravely, as if they were about to carry the whole of heaven.

And the Shepherd said to me, “Why are you reasoning within yourself, and perplexed, and bringing grief on yourself? Whatever you cannot grasp, do not attempt, if you are a man of understanding. Ask the Lord instead, so that you may receive understanding and grasp these things.

“You cannot see what is behind you, but you do see what is in front of you. So let alone what you cannot see, and do not torture yourself. But what you do see, make yourself master of that, and do not pry into the rest. I will make clear to you everything that I show you. So look now at what remains.”

I saw that six men had come, tall and glorious and alike in appearance, and they called a multitude of men. Those who came were tall men too, handsome and strong. The six men ordered them to build a tower upon the rock. And there was a great commotion among those men who had come to build the tower, as they ran here and there around the gate.

The virgins standing around the gate kept telling the men to hurry on with the building of the tower. And the virgins had stretched out their hands, as if they were about to receive something from the men.
Then the six men ordered stones to come up from a certain deep place and go into the building of the tower. And ten stones came up, square and bright, and not hewn.

The six men called the virgins and ordered them to carry all the stones that were to go into the building of the tower. The virgins were to pass through the gate with the stones and hand them to the men who were to build the tower.
The virgins loaded one another with the first ten stones, the ones that had come up from the deep, and together they carried them, one stone at a time.

Just as they had stood together around the gate, so they carried. Those who seemed to be strong had gone in under the corners of the stone, and the others had gone in under its sides. In this way they carried all the stones. They brought them through the gate, as they had been ordered, and handed them to the men for the tower. And the men took the stones and built.

The tower was built upon the great rock and above the gate. Those ten stones were fitted together, and they filled the whole rock. They became the foundation of the building of the tower. And the rock and the gate carried the whole tower.

After the ten stones, another twenty stones came up from the deep. These too were fitted into the building of the tower, carried by the virgins just as the first ones had been. After these, thirty-five came up, and these were fitted into the tower in the same way. After these, another forty stones came up, and all of them were put into the building of the tower. So there were four courses in the foundations of the tower.

Then the stones stopped coming up from the deep, and the builders also stopped for a little while. And the six men again commanded the great crowd to bring stones from the mountains for the building of the tower.

So stones of many colors were brought from all the mountains, hewn by the men, and they were handed to the virgins. The virgins carried them through the gate and handed them in for the building of the tower. And when the stones of many colors were set in the building, they all alike became white, and they changed their many colors.

But some stones were handed in for the building by the men, and these did not become bright. As they were when they were set there, so they were found. For they had not been handed in by the virgins, and they had not been carried through the gate. So these stones were unsightly in the building of the tower.
When the six men saw the unsightly stones in the building, they ordered them to be taken out and carried back down to their own place, the place they had been brought from.

And they said to the men who were bringing in the stones, “You are not to hand in any stones for the building at all. Set them down beside the tower, so that the virgins may carry them through the gate and hand them in for the building. For if they are not carried through the gate by the hands of these virgins, they cannot change their colors. So do not labor in vain.”

On that day the building came to an end, but the tower was not completed, for it was to be built up further. So there was a pause in the building. The six men ordered all the builders to withdraw for a little while and rest. But they commanded the virgins not to withdraw from the tower. It seemed to me that the virgins had been left behind to guard the tower.

When they had all withdrawn and were at rest, I said to the Shepherd, “Sir, why was the building of the tower not finished?” He said, “The tower cannot be completed yet, not until its lord comes and tests this building, so that if any stones are found to be rotten, he may change them. For the tower is being built according to his will.”

“Sir,” I said, “I would like to know what this building of the tower is, and about the rock and the gate, the mountains and the virgins. I would like to know about the stones that came up from the deep and were not hewn, but went into the building just as they were. And why were ten stones laid first in the foundations, then twenty, then thirty-five, then forty? And what of the stones that went into the building and were taken out again and put back in their own place? Set my soul at rest about all these things, sir, and make them known to me.”

He said, “If your eagerness is not found to be empty, you will know everything. For after a few days we will come here, and you will see the rest of what is to come upon this tower, and you will know all the parables exactly.”

After a few days we came to the place where we had sat. He said to me, “Let us go to the tower, for the owner of the tower is coming to inspect it.” So we came to the tower, and there was no one beside it at all, only the virgins.
The Shepherd asked the virgins whether the master of the tower had arrived. They said that he was about to come and inspect the building.
And look, after a little while I saw an array of many men coming. In the middle was a man so tall that he rose higher than the tower.

The six men who were in charge of the building walked with him on his right and on his left. All those who had worked on the building were with him, and around him were many other glorious ones. The virgins who were keeping watch over the tower ran up and kissed him, and they began to walk near him around the tower.
That man inspected the building closely, so closely that he felt each stone, one by one. He held a rod in his hand, and he struck every single stone that had been built in.

And when he struck them, some of them turned black as soot. Some turned scabby, some had cracks, some were stunted, some were neither white nor black, some were rough and did not fit with the other stones, and some had many spots. These were the different kinds of rotten stones that were found in the building.
So he ordered all of these to be taken out of the tower and set down beside the tower, and other stones to be brought and put in their place.

The builders asked him from which mountain he wanted stones to be brought and put in their place. He did not order them to be brought from the mountains. He ordered them to be brought from a plain that lay nearby.
So the plain was dug, and bright stones were found, square ones, and some round ones too. Every stone that was in that plain was brought, and the virgins carried them through the gate.

The square stones were hewn and set in the place of those that had been taken out. But the round ones were not set in the building, because they were hard to hew and the hewing went slowly. They were set down beside the tower, since they were going to be hewn and set in the building, for they were very bright.

When the glorious man, the lord of the whole tower, had finished these things, he called the Shepherd to him. He handed over to him all the stones that lay beside the tower, the ones that had been cast out of the building, and he said to him,
“Clean these stones carefully, and set in the building of the tower those that can fit with the rest. But those that do not fit, throw far away from the tower.”
When he had given the Shepherd these orders, he went away from the tower with all those who had come with him. But the virgins stood around the tower, keeping watch over it.

I said to the Shepherd, “How can these stones go into the building of the tower, when they have been rejected?” He answered me, “Do you see these stones?” “I see them, sir,” I said. He said, “I myself will hew the greater part of these stones and put them into the building, and they will fit with the rest of the stones.”

“Sir,” I said, “how can they fill the same space once they have been cut down?” He answered me, “Those that are found to be small will be put in the middle of the building. Those that are larger will be set on the outside, and they will hold the small ones together.”

After saying this to me, he went on, “Let us go. After two days let us come and clean these stones and put them into the building. For everything around the tower must be cleaned. Otherwise the master may come suddenly and find the place around the tower dirty, and be angry. Then these stones will not go into the building of the tower, and I will seem careless in the master’s eyes.”
After two days we came to the tower, and he said to me, “Let us inspect all the stones and see which ones can go into the building.” I said to him, “Sir, let us inspect them.”

We began with the black stones and inspected them first. As they were when they were put out of the building, so they were found. And the Shepherd ordered them to be carried away from the tower and set apart.

Next he inspected the scabby stones. He took many of them and hewed them, and he ordered the virgins to take them up and put them into the building. The virgins took them up and set them in the middle of the building of the tower. The rest he ordered to be put with the black stones, for these too were found to be black.

Next he inspected the stones that had cracks. He hewed many of these too, and he ordered that the virgins carry them away into the building. They were set on the outside, because they were found to be sounder. The rest could not be hewn, because their cracks were so many. For this reason they were cast out from the building of the tower.

Next he inspected the stunted stones. Many among them were found to be black, and some had developed great cracks. He ordered these too to be put with the stones that had been cast out. But the ones left over he cleaned and hewed, and he ordered them to be set in the building. The virgins took them up and fitted them into the middle of the building of the tower, for they were weaker.

Next he inspected the stones that were half white and half black. Many of them were found to be black, and he ordered these too to be taken away with the stones that had been cast out. All the rest were taken up by the virgins. Because they were white, the virgins themselves fitted them into the building. They were set on the outside, because they were found to be sound, so that they could hold the stones set in the middle. For nothing at all had been cut away from them.

Next he inspected the rough, hard stones. A few of them were cast out because they could not be hewn, for they were found to be very hard. The rest of them were hewn, and the virgins took them up and fitted them into the middle of the building of the tower, for they were weaker.

Next he inspected the stones that had the spots. A very few of these had turned black, and they were cast out with the others. Those left over were found to be bright and sound, and the virgins fitted these too into the building. They were set on the outside because of their strength.
Then he came to inspect the white, round stones, and he said to me, “What are we to do about these stones?” “Sir,” I said, “what do I know?” He said, “So you have no thought about them at all?”

“Sir,” I said, “I do not have this craft. I am not a stonecutter, and I cannot work it out.” He said, “Do you not see that they are very round? If I want to make them square, a great deal must be cut away from them. Yet some of them must of necessity be set in the building.”

“Sir,” I said, “if it is a necessity, why do you torment yourself? Why not choose the ones you want for the building and fit them into it?” He chose the larger, bright ones from among them and hewed them, and the virgins took them up and fitted them into the outer parts of the building.

The rest, those left over, were taken up and put back in the plain they had been brought from. But they were not cast out. “For,” said the Shepherd, “a little of the tower still remains to be built. And the master of the tower wants all these stones to be fitted into the building, because they are very bright.”

Then twelve women were called. They were very lovely in appearance. They were dressed in black and girded, with their shoulders bare and their hair hanging loose. These women seemed to me to be wild. The Shepherd ordered them to take up the stones that had been cast out of the building and carry them away to the mountains they had been brought from.

Cheerfully the women took up all the stones, carried them away, and set them down where they had been taken from. When all the stones had been taken up and not a stone lay around the tower any longer, the Shepherd said to me, “Let us go around the tower and see whether there is any defect in it.” So I went around it with him.

When the Shepherd saw that the tower was beautiful in its building, he was very cheerful. For the tower was built in such a way that when I saw it, I longed for its building. It was built as if from a single stone, with not one joint in it. The stone looked as if it had been carved out of the rock, for it seemed to me to be all one stone.

I too was cheerful as I walked with him and saw such good things. Then the Shepherd said to me, “Go and bring lime and finely crushed pottery, so that I may fill up the hollows left by the stones that were taken up and put into the building. For everything around the tower must be made level.”

I did as he ordered and brought them to him. “Assist me,” he said, “and the work will soon be finished.” So he filled up the hollows left by the stones that had gone into the building, and he ordered the place around the tower to be swept and made clean.
The virgins took brooms and swept. They cleared all the filth away from the tower and sprinkled water, and the place of the tower became cheerful and most beautiful.
The Shepherd said to me, “Everything has been cleaned. If the lord comes to visit the tower, he has nothing to blame us for.” When he had said this, he wanted to go.

But I caught hold of his bag and began to adjure him by the Lord to explain to me what he had shown me. He said to me, “I am busy for a little while, and then I will explain everything to you. Wait for me here until I come.”
